levels.name: A1 — Beginner
levels.description: First steps in Mandarin: greetings, numbers, basic verbs and questions.

topics.title: Pinyin Tones
topics.description: Train your ear for the four tones — the foundation of Mandarin

guide.intro: Mandarin uses pitch to tell words apart. The same syllable in a different tone is a different word — get tones in your ear before you build sentences.

sections.text: Why tones matter
English uses pitch for emotion ("REAL-ly?" vs "really."). Mandarin uses pitch for meaning. "mā" (mom) and "mà" (scold) are not the same word — they're as different as "cat" and "dog".
The four tones + neutral
When you practice, exaggerate. Tones feel embarrassing at first — that's how you know you're doing them right.
Sandhi: tones that shift
Two real-world tweaks: (1) when two 3rd tones meet, the first becomes 2nd: nǐ + hǎo → ní hǎo. (2) 不 (bù) becomes bú before a 4th tone (bú shì). (3) 一 (yī) becomes yí before 4th, yì otherwise.

lessons.title: Meet the four tones
lessons.description: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th + neutral

exercises.prompt: How many tones does Mandarin have (not counting neutral)?
exercises.explanation: Four tones — 1st (flat), 2nd (rising), 3rd (dip), 4th (falling). Plus an unstressed neutral tone.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 1st tone (high and flat)?
exercises.explanation: The macron (¯) over the vowel signals 1st tone — held high and steady.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 2nd tone (rising)?
exercises.explanation: The acute accent (´) signals 2nd tone — pitch rises like "huh?"

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 3rd tone (dip down then up)?
exercises.explanation: The háček (ˇ) signals 3rd tone — pitch dips then comes back up.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 4th tone (sharp falling)?
exercises.explanation: The grave accent (`) signals 4th tone — short, falling, often emphatic.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 媽 is high and flat — the 1st tone. It means "mother."

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 馬 (horse) dips down then back up — the 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 罵 (scold) falls sharply from high to low — the 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: tone to its meaning
Type the pinyin for "horse" (3rd tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 馬 = mǎ. Use the ˇ mark for 3rd tone (or write "ma3" in numeric pinyin).

exercises.prompt: Mandarin's neutral tone is best described as ___
options: Unstressed and light, often on the second syllable
A 5th tone with its own contour
exercises.answer: Unstressed and light, often on the second syllable
exercises.explanation: Neutral tone has no mark — said quickly, lightly. Common in particles (嗎, 呢) and repeated syllables (媽媽).

exercises.prompt: Which syllable is most likely neutral tone?
exercises.explanation: In doubled family terms like 媽媽, 爸爸, 哥哥 — the second syllable is neutral.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "mother" (1st tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 媽 = mā. First tone, held high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which character matches the 2nd tone (rising) ma-syllable?
exercises.explanation: 麻 (má) is 2nd tone — rising. Means "hemp" or "numb".

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "to scold" (4th tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 罵 = mà. Fourth tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 麻 (má) — 2nd tone, rising. Means hemp.

exercises.prompt: Two syllables can have the same letters and the same initial — only the ___ makes them different words.
exercises.explanation: Tones are phonemic in Mandarin — they distinguish meaning.
媽 (mā) — flat high tone, means "mother."

exercises.prompt: The mark ¯ over a vowel signals tone number ___
exercises.explanation: The macron (¯) is the 1st tone mark — held high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which tone has the háček (ˇ) mark?
exercises.explanation: The háček ˇ marks 3rd tone — pitch dips then rises.

lessons.description: Flat-high vs rising

exercises.prompt: 1st tone is held high and flat. 2nd tone does what?
exercises.explanation: 2nd tone rises from mid to high — same melody as English "huh?"

exercises.prompt: bā vs bá — which one is the 2nd tone?
exercises.explanation: bā 八 (eight) is 1st tone, flat. bá 拔 (to pull) is 2nd tone, rising.

exercises.prompt: fā vs fá — which means "to send / hair" (1st tone)?

lessons.title: 3rd vs 4th tone
lessons.description: Dipping vs falling

exercises.prompt: How does the 3rd tone move?
options: Dips down then comes back up
exercises.answer: Dips down then comes back up
exercises.explanation: Mid → low → mid. In careful speech the dip is dramatic; in quick speech it's often a low "half-3rd".

exercises.prompt: mǎi vs mài — which means "to buy"?
exercises.explanation: 買 mǎi = buy (dipping). 賣 mài = sell (falling). Remember: 賣 has the extra 十 on top — "goods piled up to sell."

exercises.prompt: kàn means "to look/watch." What tone is it?
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — sharp falling. (kǎn 砍 "to chop" with 3rd tone is a different word.)

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 買 dips and rises — 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 賣 falls sharply — 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — sharp, falling 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 那 nà = that — 4th tone. Compare 哪 nǎ = which — 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: 3rd vs 4th — pair to meaning
Type the pinyin for "to look/watch":
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — 4th tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: You hear a single short, falling syllable. What tone is it most likely?
exercises.explanation: Short + falling = 4th. Native speakers often shorten 4th tone in casual speech.

exercises.prompt: 4th tone moves ___
options: Sharp falling from high to low
exercises.answer: Sharp falling from high to low
exercises.explanation: 4th tone is the dramatic crash — high to low, abrupt.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 賣 ("to sell"):
exercises.explanation: 賣 mài — 4th tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 那 ("that"):

exercises.explanation: Same initial m + ai. Tones change meaning entirely.

exercises.prompt: Which tone is often shortened in fast speech?
Order tones from 1 to 4 using the standard ma-syllable

exercises.explanation: 媽 (1st) → 麻 (2nd) → 馬 (3rd) → 罵 (4th). The classic teaching set.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 看 ("look/watch"):

lessons.title: 3rd-tone sandhi
lessons.description: How 你好 actually sounds

exercises.prompt: What happens when two 3rd tones meet (3rd-tone sandhi)?
exercises.explanation: 3 + 3 → 2 + 3. So nǐ + hǎo is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo.

exercises.prompt: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo. What does it sound like?
exercises.explanation: First 3rd tone shifts to 2nd. Pinyin keeps the original marks; your mouth does the shift.

exercises.prompt: 很好 (hěn hǎo, "very good") — what does it sound like?
exercises.explanation: Two 3rd tones in a row → first becomes 2nd. Said hén hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 你好 — the most common hello. Note the sandhi: written nǐ hǎo, said ní hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 很好 — said hén hǎo because of 3rd-tone sandhi.

exercises.prompt: How is sandhi written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: Standard convention: write nǐ hǎo, say ní hǎo. The shift is in your mouth, not on the page.

exercises.prompt: Three 3rd tones in 我也好 (wǒ yě hǎo, "I'm also good"). The first two shift. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Chains of 3rd tones: most become 2nd, only the last stays 3rd. wǒ yě hǎo → wó yé hǎo.

exercises.prompt: written vs spoken
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 可以 ("can / may") — written kě yǐ, said ké yǐ (sandhi).

exercises.prompt: Does sandhi apply across pauses/sentence breaks?
options: Always, every time two 3rd tones touch
Only within a single word or tight phrase
exercises.answer: Only within a single word or tight phrase
exercises.explanation: Sandhi follows the rhythm of the phrase. If you'd naturally pause between the syllables, no shift.

exercises.prompt: 3-3 sandhi means ___ becomes ___
exercises.explanation: 3+3 → 2+3. Written marks stay; the change is spoken.

exercises.prompt: How is 很好 actually pronounced?
exercises.explanation: 3+3 → 2+3. Written hěn hǎo, spoken hén hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase undergoes 3-3 sandhi?
exercises.explanation: Only when two 3rd tones touch within a phrase.

exercises.prompt: Write "you good" using two characters
Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 可以 — written kě yǐ, said ké yǐ (sandhi).

exercises.prompt: Sandhi marks are ___
options: Mental — not shown on the page
exercises.answer: Mental — not shown on the page
exercises.explanation: Standard convention keeps the original 3rd-tone marks. The shift lives in the mouth.

exercises.prompt: Three 3rd tones — only the LAST stays 3rd. Type the spoken version of 我也好:
exercises.explanation: Chains shift: most syllables become 2nd, only the last keeps 3rd.

exercises.prompt: Does sandhi apply across a pause/comma?
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 我很好 with 3-3 sandhi: wó hěn hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT affected by 3-3 sandhi?
exercises.explanation: 明天 mingtiān — 2nd + 1st. No two 3rd tones to clash.

lessons.title: 不 and 一 sandhi
lessons.description: When bù becomes bú and yī becomes yí/yì

exercises.prompt: 不 (bù) means "not." What's its default tone?
exercises.explanation: 不 is normally 4th tone — bù. It only shifts before another 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: 不 + 是 (shì, "is") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 becomes 2nd: bú shì "is not."

exercises.prompt: 不 + 來 (lái, 2nd tone, "come") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before any non-4th tone, 不 stays 4th: bù lái "not come."

exercises.prompt: 一 (yī) means "one." Before a 4th tone like 個 (gè), it becomes...
exercises.explanation: 一 + 4th → yí. So 一個 is yí ge in speech.

exercises.prompt: 一 + 起 (qǐ, 3rd tone, "rise") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before non-4th tones (1st, 2nd, 3rd), 一 becomes 4th: yì qǐ "together."

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 不是 — 不 shifts to 2nd tone before 是 (4th).

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 一個 = yí ge — one (thing). 個 is neutral in speech but counts as 4th for sandhi.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 一起 = yì qǐ — together. 一 became 4th before 3rd-tone 起.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不 + 要 (yào, 4th, "want") in speech?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 becomes 2nd: bú yào "don't want / don't."

exercises.prompt: When does 一 NOT shift tone?
options: When standing alone or saying numbers in sequence
exercises.answer: When standing alone or saying numbers in sequence
exercises.explanation: Counting (yī, èr, sān...) or year numbers (一九九九) keeps 一 as 1st tone. Sandhi only kicks in when 一 leads into another syllable as part of a meaning unit.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不 + 對 (duì, 4th, "correct")?
exercises.explanation: Before 4th tone, 不 shifts to 2nd: bú duì.

exercises.prompt: Before any non-4th tone, 不 stays ___
exercises.explanation: 不 + 1st/2nd/3rd → bù (4th, unchanged). Only 不 + 4th → bú.

exercises.prompt: 一 + 天 (tiān, 1st, "day") becomes ___
exercises.explanation: Before non-4th tones, 一 shifts to 4th: yì tiān.

exercises.prompt: How is 一年 (one year) spoken?
exercises.explanation: 一 + 2nd (年 nián) → 一 becomes 4th: yì nián.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 不 + 2nd-tone 來 → unchanged: bù lái.

exercises.prompt: 不 changes tone only when followed by ___
exercises.explanation: Sandhi rule for 不: only before 4th tones does it shift to 2nd.

exercises.prompt: How is 一千 (one thousand) spoken?
exercises.explanation: 一 + 1st (千 qiān) → 一 becomes 4th.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: Before 4th tone 要, 不 → bú.

exercises.prompt: In counting (yī, èr, sān…) what tone does 一 keep?
exercises.explanation: Sandhi doesn't apply when 一 is standing alone or counting.

exercises.prompt: Order: bú shì → before this 4th-tone character, 不 shifts to 2nd

topics.title: Pinyin Sounds
topics.description: The tricky consonants and vowels of pinyin — the ones English doesn't have

guide.intro: Pinyin is the romanization that lets you type, look up, and pronounce Mandarin. Most letters do what you'd expect — but a handful are traps for English speakers.

sections.text: Initials: where sound starts
Mandarin has three pairs that English speakers mix up: zh/ch/sh (retroflex — curl your tongue back) vs z/c/s (sibilant — tongue flat). Plus j/q/x — like Italian's c/g — always followed by i or ü.

rows: j in 'jar' with tongue curled back

sections.text: j / q / x — the i/ü trio
j, q, x are softer than zh, ch, sh — tongue stays forward. They only ever appear before i or ü. After j/q/x, ü is written as plain u (so 居 is jū, but the vowel is really ü).
qù sounds like "chü" — NOT "q-you" or "tsoo." The q is a soft "ch" and ù is a rounded "ee" with pursed lips.
Finals: the trap vowels
Some finals don't match their spelling. -ian sounds like "yen," not "yan." -uan after j/q/x/y is really -üan (so 元 yuán = "yu-en"). -eng has a back "ung" feel vs -en which is light and forward.

rows.translation: to see
yuan (currency)
to listen

lessons.title: Initials: zh/ch/sh vs z/c/s
lessons.description: Retroflex (tongue curled) vs flat sibilants

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between zh and z?
options: zh is retroflex (tongue curls back); z is flat
z is retroflex; zh is flat
exercises.answer: zh is retroflex (tongue curls back); z is flat
exercises.explanation: zh/ch/sh = tongue curled back (retroflex). z/c/s = tongue flat. Easy to mix up; speakers in southern China often merge them.

exercises.prompt: 知 ("to know") is zhī. How is 資 ("resource") spelled?
exercises.explanation: 知 zhī uses the retroflex zh; 資 zī uses flat z. Same vowel, different tongue position.

exercises.prompt: Which English sound is closest to Mandarin c (as in 詞 cí)?
exercises.explanation: c is the "ts" cluster — no h, no curl. Don't read it as English "c."

exercises.prompt: 吃 ("to eat") is chī. How is 詞 ("word") spelled?
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī uses retroflex ch; 詞 cí uses flat c. Common minimal pair.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: Retroflex zh — tongue curled back.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 四 sì — flat s, no tongue curl, 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 是 shì — retroflex sh, tongue curls back.

exercises.prompt: retroflex vs flat partners
Type the pinyin for 是 ("is"):
exercises.explanation: 是 shì — retroflex sh, 4th tone. The most common verb "to be."

exercises.prompt: Which is a fact about southern-China accents?
options: They distinguish zh/z more carefully than the north
They often merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s
exercises.answer: They often merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s
exercises.explanation: Many southern speakers (Shanghai, Taiwan, etc.) don't distinguish retroflex from flat — they pronounce 是 closer to sì. Standard Mandarin (北京話) keeps them apart.

exercises.prompt: Which sound requires tongue curled back?
exercises.explanation: zh/ch/sh are retroflex — tongue tip curls back.

exercises.prompt: Which is the flat sibilant partner of sh?
exercises.explanation: s is the flat partner; sh is retroflex.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 吃 ("to eat"):
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī — retroflex ch, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 詞 ("word"):
exercises.explanation: 詞 cí — flat c, 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 私 sī — flat s, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Native speakers from which region most consistently distinguish zh/z?
exercises.explanation: Northern Mandarin (Beijing) keeps retroflex distinct from flat.
吃 chī — retroflex ch.

exercises.prompt: c in Mandarin pinyin sounds like ___
exercises.explanation: c = ts, never English c. No aspiration mistake.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 資 zī — flat z, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 知 ("to know"):
exercises.explanation: 知 zhī — retroflex zh, 1st tone.

lessons.title: Tricky j/q/x + i/ü
lessons.description: When 'u' is really 'ü' and q isn't English q

exercises.prompt: j, q, x can ONLY be followed by which vowels?
exercises.explanation: Hard rule: j/q/x never appear before a, o, u, e by themselves. They only pair with i (as in ji, qi, xi) or ü (written u, as in ju, qu, xu).

exercises.prompt: 居 is spelled "jū." What's the actual vowel sound?
options: ü (rounded ee — say ee with pursed lips)
exercises.answer: ü (rounded ee — say ee with pursed lips)
exercises.explanation: After j/q/x/y, ü drops its dots: jū looks like "ju" but is really jü. Make ee with rounded lips.

exercises.prompt: 去 ("to go") is qù. How would you describe the sound?
exercises.explanation: q is a soft, forward "ch" — not the English q. ù is the rounded-ee. So qù is more like "chü" than anything in English.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is actually pronounced with ü?
exercises.explanation: ju, qu, xu, yu are all really jü, qü, xü, yü. zhu, chu, shu, zu, cu, su use real u.

exercises.prompt: What does the x in Mandarin sound like?
options: soft sh — tongue forward, like a German "ich" softened
exercises.answer: soft sh — tongue forward, like a German "ich" softened
exercises.explanation: x = a forward, light "sh." Tongue near the roof of the mouth, no curling. 謝 xiè ("thanks") and 學 xué are common.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: qù — soft ch + ü, 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: xué — soft x + ü-e diphthong, 2nd tone (rising). "To study/learn."

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: jī — soft j (like "jee"), 1st tone. Don't confuse with retroflex zhī.

topics.title: How Characters Work
topics.description: Chinese characters are made of reusable pieces — learn to spot them

guide.intro: Chinese characters look intimidating but they're built from a small set of reusable pieces. Once you see the pattern, learning new characters speeds up.

sections.text: Characters are made of pieces

Almost every Chinese character is a combination of smaller components. Some components are simple characters in their own right; others (radicals) only appear as parts of larger characters. Recognizing the pieces makes the whole easier.

rows.translation: good
bright
forest
rest (a person leaning on a tree)

sections.text: Radicals as meaning clues

About 200 "radicals" group characters by meaning. If a character contains 氵 (water), it likely relates to water (rivers, drinking, thirst). 心 (heart) → emotions. 口 (mouth) → speech and eating. The radical doesn't tell you the whole meaning, but it points you in the right neighborhood.

rows: 河 river, 海 sea, 江 river, 渴 thirsty
林 forest, 樹 tree, 橋 bridge
想 think, 愛 love, 急 urgent
吃 eat, 喝 drink, 叫 shout/call
你 you, 他 he, 們 plural-marker
她 she, 好 good, 媽 mom

sections.text: When you see a new character, guess at the radical first. If it has 氵 you'll be roughly right calling it water-related — that's enough to remember it.

lessons.title: Characters are made of pieces
lessons.description: Components and meaning-compounds

exercises.prompt: 好 ("good") is made of which two components?
exercises.explanation: 好 hǎo = 女 + 子 — woman with child. A traditional mnemonic for "good."

exercises.prompt: 明 ("bright") is made of which two components?
exercises.explanation: 明 míng = sun + moon = bright. One of the most famous "meaning-compound" characters.

exercises.prompt: 林 ("forest") is made of what?
exercises.explanation: Two 木 (tree) = 林 lín (forest/grove). Three trees = 森 sēn (dense forest). Repeat for emphasis.

exercises.prompt: Which character means "to rest" (a person leaning on a tree)?
exercises.explanation: 休 xiū = 亻 (person) + 木 (tree). Pictorial: a person resting against a tree.

exercises.prompt: character to its components
你 ("you") contains which component on the left?
exercises.explanation: 亻 is the "person" radical (a flattened form of 人). It shows up in many person-related characters: 你, 他, 們, 休, 體.

exercises.prompt: Why do components matter for learning?
options: They don't — just memorize each character whole
They group characters by meaning and pronunciation, making recall faster
They only matter for traditional characters
exercises.answer: They group characters by meaning and pronunciation, making recall faster
exercises.explanation: Most characters fall into a pattern: one piece hints at meaning (radical), one hints at sound. Knowing this turns rote memorization into educated guessing.

exercises.prompt: 她 ("she") differs from 他 ("he") only by replacing which component?
exercises.explanation: 他 tā = person + 也 (the default "he"). 她 tā = woman + 也 (the gendered "she"). Same sound, different left piece.

exercises.prompt: 好 = 女 + ___ . Type the second component:
exercises.explanation: 好 hǎo = 女 (woman) + 子 (child). The traditional reading: a woman with her child = "good."

exercises.prompt: 森 ("dense forest") is made of how many 木?
exercises.explanation: 森 sēn = three 木. One tree = 木. Two = 林 (forest). Three = 森 (dense forest). Chinese character design at its most direct.

exercises.prompt: The character 男 ("man/male") combines ___
exercises.explanation: 男 = field + strength. Traditional: "the one who works the field with strength."

exercises.prompt: 好 = 女 + 子. 女 means ___
exercises.explanation: 女 = woman/female. Look for 女 on the left of many female-related characters.

exercises.prompt: Three trees stacked together (森) means ___
exercises.explanation: 一木 (tree) → 二木 (林, grove) → 三木 (森, dense forest).
林 lín — two 木. Forest/grove.

exercises.prompt: Which character means "to rest"?
exercises.explanation: 休 xiū — person leaning on a tree (亻 + 木) = rest.
明 míng = 日 (sun) + 月 (moon) = bright.

exercises.prompt: Which radical is on the LEFT of 你?
exercises.explanation: 亻 is the side form of 人 (person) — appears in many pronouns/people characters.

exercises.prompt: Order the pieces of the character 好
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 好 hǎo — 3rd tone, dipping. Combination character: woman + child.

exercises.prompt: Why do components matter?
options: They hint at meaning AND sometimes sound — making memorization easier
exercises.answer: They hint at meaning AND sometimes sound — making memorization easier

lessons.title: Common radicals
lessons.description: 氵 water, 木 wood, 心 heart, 口 mouth

exercises.prompt: 氵 is the radical for what?
exercises.explanation: 氵 is the "three-drops" form of 水 shuǐ (water). Appears on the left of water-related characters: 河 (river), 海 (sea), 渴 (thirsty).

exercises.prompt: Which character does NOT contain the water radical 氵?
exercises.explanation: 山 shān is its own pictograph (three peaks) — no 氵. 河, 海, 江 all use 氵 because they involve water.

exercises.prompt: 木 is the radical for what?
exercises.explanation: 木 mù = tree. As a radical, it marks things made of wood or related to trees: 橋 bridge, 樹 tree, 林 forest.

exercises.prompt: What does 心 mean (as a radical)?
exercises.explanation: 心 xīn = heart. Appears in characters for emotions and thinking: 想 think, 愛 love, 急 urgent, 怕 afraid.

exercises.prompt: 口 means "mouth." Which character uses it?
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī (eat) has 口 on the left — eating uses the mouth. Also 喝 (drink), 叫 (shout/call), 唱 (sing).

exercises.prompt: radical to its meaning
character to its radical
Which radical would you expect to find in a character meaning "to sing"?
exercises.explanation: 唱 chàng (to sing) has 口 — singing uses the mouth. Pattern repeats: 叫 (shout), 喊 (yell), 喝 (drink), 吃 (eat).

exercises.prompt: Which radical would you expect in 愛 ("love")?
exercises.explanation: 愛 ài contains 心 in the middle (slightly hidden in modern simplified form, very clear in traditional 愛). Love = a heart matter.

exercises.prompt: Why are radicals useful for looking up characters?
options: They're alphabetized by radical in dictionaries
Older paper dictionaries indexed all characters by their radical and stroke count
Both of the above are true
exercises.answer: Both of the above are true
exercises.explanation: Before digital tools, you found a character by identifying its radical, then counting remaining strokes. Knowing radicals = knowing how to navigate the language.

exercises.prompt: Where does the 氵 radical usually sit?
exercises.explanation: Most radicals appear on the left or top.

exercises.prompt: The radical for "mouth" is ___
exercises.explanation: 口 (kǒu) = mouth. Found in eat, drink, shout, sing.

exercises.prompt: Which character likely has the 木 radical?
exercises.explanation: 橋 has 木 — bridges were made of wood.

exercises.prompt: Which character means "to drink"?
exercises.explanation: 喝 hē — has 口 (mouth) because drinking uses the mouth.

exercises.context: The full form — 氵 is the side-form radical
exercises.explanation: 水 shuǐ — water. As a radical, becomes 氵.

exercises.prompt: The radical 心 means ___
exercises.explanation: 心 (xīn) = heart. Found in characters about emotion: 想, 愛, 怕.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 水 shuǐ — 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: Why does 唱 (sing) have 口?
exercises.explanation: Pattern: anything you do with the mouth tends to have 口.

exercises.prompt: Which character is built from THREE trees?
exercises.explanation: 森 = three 木 = dense forest.

exercises.prompt: Order the radicals: water, wood, heart, mouth
exercises.answer: 氵 木 心 口

lessons.title: Reading by radical clue
lessons.description: Guess unfamiliar characters from their radical

exercises.prompt: 渴 (kě) contains 氵 (water). What's the likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 渴 kě = thirsty. The 氵 radical hints at water; the rest gives the sound (曷 hé/gě). Confidence trick: see 氵 → bet on water.

exercises.prompt: 想 (xiǎng) has 心 (heart) on the bottom. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 想 xiǎng = to think, to want, to miss. The heart radical signals "mental/emotional" — exactly right.

exercises.prompt: 橋 (qiáo) has 木 (wood) on the left. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 橋 qiáo = bridge. Old bridges were wood — hence the radical. Pattern: 木 = something built from / made of wood.

exercises.prompt: 唱 (chàng) has 口 (mouth) on the left. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 唱 chàng = to sing. Anything you do with your mouth — speak, eat, shout, sing — tends to have 口.

exercises.prompt: 湖 (hú) has 氵 . What is it?
exercises.explanation: 湖 hú = lake. Big body of water → 氵 radical is the giveaway.

exercises.prompt: 忙 (máng) has 忄 (the side form of 心). Likely meaning category?
exercises.explanation: 忙 máng = busy (mentally occupied). 忄 is the side-form of 心 — same heart radical, different shape. Shows up in 快 (happy/fast), 怕 (afraid), 怒 (angry).

exercises.prompt: 喝 (hē) has 口. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 喝 hē = to drink. Mouth radical 口 + sound clue from 曷. Compare with 渴 kě (thirsty, water radical).

exercises.prompt: unfamiliar character → likely meaning category
You see 樹 — a character with 木 on the left. The character means ___
exercises.explanation: 樹 shù = tree. The 木 radical is the giveaway. Use this trick on every new character: find the radical, narrow the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Final tip: when you meet a new character, what should you do first?
options: Memorize the whole thing as one shape
Identify the radical to guess the meaning category
exercises.answer: Identify the radical to guess the meaning category
exercises.explanation: Radical → category → narrow guess from context. Far more efficient than rote memorization. The other components often hint at sound.

exercises.prompt: You see 河 — it has 氵. The likely meaning is ___
exercises.explanation: 河 hé = river. The 氵 radical screams "water-related."

exercises.prompt: 怕 (pà) has 忄 (heart). Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 怕 pà = afraid. Emotion → heart radical.

exercises.prompt: A character with 木 on the left is most likely related to ___
exercises.explanation: 木 radical = wood/tree-related: 樹, 林, 橋, 板.
湖 hú = lake. Water radical gives it away.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 想 xiǎng — to think. Heart radical at bottom.

exercises.prompt: If you see 忄 on the left of a character, you should guess ___
exercises.explanation: 忄 is the side form of 心 — used in many emotion words.

exercises.prompt: 樹 contains 木. The most likely meaning is ___
exercises.explanation: 樹 shù = tree. The 木 radical is the giveaway.

exercises.prompt: 吃 has 口 because eating uses the ___
exercises.explanation: 口 radical points to mouth-related actions: eat, drink, shout.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 橋 qiáo — bridge. Has 木 radical.

exercises.prompt: First step when meeting a new character?
options: Identify the radical to guess the meaning category
exercises.answer: Identify the radical to guess the meaning category

guide.intro: Mandarin has only a handful of greetings to learn — but the tones really matter. Here's what to know before you start.

sections.text: The four tones

Every Mandarin syllable has one of four pitched tones (plus a neutral "fifth" tone). The same syllable means different things depending on tone — so "mā", "má", "mǎ", and "mà" are four different words.
Hello: 你好 (nǐ hǎo)
你 means "you" and 好 means "good". Put them together for "you good?" — the standard hello, usable any time of day.
When two 3rd-tone syllables stack like nǐ hǎo, the first one shifts up to a 2nd tone in speech (ní hǎo). It still gets written as nǐ hǎo.
你 (nǐ) vs 您 (nín)
您 is the polite form of "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers. 你 is everyday/casual. Both pronounced almost the same.

sections.text: How are you?
To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just add 嗎 (ma) at the end. So 你好 ("you're good") + 嗎 = 你好嗎? ("are you good?").

topics.title: Numbers

guide.intro: Mandarin numbers are wonderfully regular — once you know 1 to 10 and the word for "ten", you can build every number up to 99.

sections.text: One to ten
Building 11–99
After ten, numbers are built like math problems. Read characters left to right, multiplying anything before 十 and adding anything after.
Same trick goes further: 一百 (one hundred), 一千 (one thousand), 一萬 (ten thousand) — but Chinese groups large numbers in 萬 (10,000) rather than thousands.
Two: 二 vs 兩
Mandarin has two words for "two". 二 (èr) is the digit — used in counting, math, and phone numbers. 兩 (liǎng) means "a pair of" — used before measure words and quantities.

rows.translation: twenty (the number)
two people (with measure word)

sections.text: Asking how many
幾 (jǐ) asks "how many?" for small expected counts (under ~10). 多少 (duō shǎo) asks "how much/many?" for any quantity, including money and big numbers.

guide.intro: Mandarin has no verb conjugation, no plural endings, no genders, and no articles. Once you know the word order, the language gets out of your way.

sections.text: Word order: subject – verb – object
Just like English, a basic sentence puts the subject first, the verb second, and the object last.

rows.translation: I drink tea.
He eats rice.
I love you.

sections.text: Pronouns are simple
他 (he) and 她 (she) are pronounced exactly the same — only the writing changes. In speech, listeners use context.
The verb 是 (shì)
是 means "to be" — but only for nouns connecting to other nouns ("I am a student"). For adjectives, you don't use 是; you use 很 (hěn) instead, which means "very" but is often a placeholder.

rows.translation: I am a student.
I am good. (no 是!)

sections.text: Negation: 不 vs 沒
Use 不 (bù) for negating present and future actions, and for adjectives. Use 沒 (méi) for past actions and for the verb 有 ("to have").

rows.source: 我 不 喝 茶。
rows.translation: I don't drink tea.

rows.source: 我 沒 有 錢。
rows.translation: I don't have money.

sections.text: No tenses!
Mandarin verbs do not change form for past, present, or future. Time is shown by adding a time word (yesterday, tomorrow) or particles like 了 (le) for completion.

rows.source: 昨天 我 吃 米飯。
rows.translation: Yesterday I ate rice.

rows.source: 明天 我 吃 米飯。
rows.translation: Tomorrow I will eat rice.

exercises.answer: Verb itself, optionally negated with 不

exercises.prompt: the right negation: 我 ___ 有 錢。(I don't have money.)

他 (he) and 她 (she) — what's the difference?
options: Different meanings (one is for adults, one for kids)
exercises.explanation: In speech, you can't tell — context decides. The 女 radical in 她 marks female; 它 (also tā) is for animals/things.

the sibling
Why does Mandarin distinguish 哥哥 vs 弟弟 instead of using one word for "brother"?

exercises.explanation: Chinese family terms encode age. You can't say "brother" without specifying older or younger — culture baked into vocabulary.

topics.title: Common verbs
topics.description: Go, eat, want, like, see, listen

guide.intro: Mandarin verbs never change form. The same character is used for all persons and all times — context (and time words) does the heavy lifting.

sections.text: One verb, every form
Compare with English: "go / goes / went / will go" — Mandarin uses 去 for all of them. The action stays put; you add words around it.

rows.translation: I go / I am going.
He goes.
We go.
I went yesterday.

sections.text: Want vs. would-like: 要 / 想 / 喜歡
These three look interchangeable in English but have a clear pecking order in Mandarin.

rows: I want / I will (decisive, ordering food)
I would like / I am thinking about

rows.translation: I want coffee. (I'll have)

rows.source: 我 想 喝 咖啡。
rows.translation: I would like to drink coffee.
I like coffee.

sections.text: Completion: the 了 particle
Adding 了 (le) after a verb signals an action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to past tense — but it's really an aspect marker, not a tense.

rows.translation: I am eating.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 飯。
rows.translation: I ate. / I have eaten.

sections.text: Don't sprinkle 了 everywhere — for adjectives ("I am happy") or stative verbs, you don't use it. Save it for completed actions.

topics.title: Time
topics.description: Days, hours, and when things happen

guide.intro: Time words go at the start of a sentence or right after the subject — never at the end like English. "Tomorrow I go" is the natural Mandarin order.

sections.text: Days are math
Days of the week are 星期 (xīngqī, "week") + the digit. So 星期一 is week-1 (Monday), 星期二 is week-2 (Tuesday), and so on through 星期六. Sunday is the odd one out: 星期天 or 星期日.
Telling time
Hours use 點 (diǎn, "o'clock"), minutes use 分 (fēn). Half-past is 半 (bàn). "Quarter" is 一刻 (yí kè) for :15 and 三刻 for :45.

rows.translation: 3 o'clock

sections.text: Time-words come first
In Mandarin, time goes before the verb. Compare:

rows.source: 我 明天 去 學校。
rows.translation: I am going to school tomorrow.

rows.source: 他 今天 不 來。
rows.translation: He is not coming today.

sections.text: A handy memory trick: Chinese says time in big-to-small order — year, month, day, hour, minute. The opposite of how dates are spoken in English.

topics.title: Questions
topics.description: Who, what, when, why, how

guide.intro: Mandarin questions are unusually friendly to learners — there's no auxiliary "do/does", no inversion. The word order stays the same as a statement.

sections.text: The 嗎 particle
For yes/no questions, take a statement and add 嗎 (ma) at the end. That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

rows.translation: You drink tea.

rows.source: 你 喝 茶 嗎？
rows.translation: Do you drink tea?

sections.text: Question words stay put
For information questions (who, what, where), put the question word exactly where the answer would go. No fronting like English.

rows.translation: Who are you? (You are who?)
What are you drinking?
Where are you?
Why is he coming?

sections.text: Common question words
A-not-A questions
A second way to ask yes/no questions: repeat the verb with 不 between. It's a touch more direct than 嗎.

rows.source: 你 是不是 學生？
rows.translation: Are you a student or not?
Do you drink tea or not?

sections.text: Don't mix patterns: 你是不是學生嗎？ is wrong. Pick one of the two question forms.

exercises.prompt: Type the particle that turns a statement into a yes/no question:
exercises.explanation: 嗎 ma — yes/no question particle, sentence-final.

exercises.prompt: Can you combine A-not-A with 嗎?

exercises.prompt: What does "走路" (zǒu lù) mean?
Which means "by car"?
"地鐵" (dì tiě) means ___
the transport
What does "腳踏車" (zì xíng chē) mean?
exercises.explanation: 腳踏車 literally "self-go-vehicle" — a vehicle that goes by itself (i.e., no engine, just legs).

exercises.prompt: "計程車" (chū zū chē) means ___
exercises.explanation: 出租 = rent out, 車 = vehicle. A "rental car" — by the trip.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 走 = walk, 路 = road. "Walk the road" — go on foot.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I take the subway to school"
exercises.answer: 我 坐 地鐵 去 學校
exercises.explanation: 坐 (zuò) = sit/take (transport). 坐 + vehicle + 去 + place = take (vehicle) to (place).

exercises.prompt: What does "騎" (qí) refer to as a verb?
exercises.explanation: 騎腳踏車 (ride a bike), 騎馬 (ride a horse). For cars, use 開 (drive). For taxis/buses, use 坐 (sit/take).

exercises.prompt: "開車" (kāi chē) means ___
exercises.explanation: 開 = open/start. "Start the vehicle" — drive.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
"Turn left" — which is correct?
exercises.explanation: Mandarin direction phrase: 向 (toward) + 左 (left) + 轉 (turn). Word order differs from English; 轉左 is a literal back-translation that sounds off.

exercises.prompt: "Go straight" — pick the right one:
exercises.explanation: 走 (walk/go) is used for directions on foot: 直走 (straight + walk). Using 去 (go to a destination) for "go straight" is a Chenglish slip — 去 takes a destination, not a manner.

exercises.prompt: Type the character meaning "sit / take (transport)":
exercises.explanation: 坐 zuò — sit; also "take (a vehicle)."

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 地鐵 — subway.

exercises.prompt: Which transport verb is for bicycles/horses?
exercises.explanation: 騎 — straddle and ride.

exercises.prompt: Build "I drive to the school"
exercises.answer: 我 開 車 去 學校

exercises.prompt: "計程車" means ___
exercises.explanation: 出租 (rent out) + 車 (vehicle).

exercises.prompt: Which means "by subway"?
exercises.explanation: 坐 + transport = take.

exercises.prompt: Which means "red"?
Which means "blue"?
"黃" (huáng) means ___
the color
Which color is associated with luck and celebration in Chinese culture?
exercises.explanation: Red signals luck, joy, and prosperity. New Year decorations, wedding dresses, and 紅包 (red envelopes for cash gifts) are all red.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 紅 (hóng, second tone — rising). Used in many compound words: 紅色 (red color), 紅茶 (black tea, literally "red tea").

exercises.prompt: Color names usually combine with ___ to mean "X color"
exercises.explanation: 色 (sè) = color. 紅色 = red color. You can sometimes drop 色 in fixed phrases.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My book is red"
exercises.answer: 我 的 書 是 紅 色

exercises.prompt: Which means "yellow color"?
exercises.explanation: Color word + 色. Note: 黃色 in some contexts (films, websites) also implies "adult content" — like English "blue" used for similar reasons.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 藍 (lán) — blue. 籃 (lán) — basket (as in 籃球, basketball). Same sound, different characters.

exercises.prompt: "藍" (lán) means ___
Type the character meaning "red":
exercises.explanation: 紅 hóng.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Which means "green"?
Build "The apple is red"
exercises.answer: 蘋果 是 紅 色

exercises.prompt: To form "X-colored," add ___ after the color word
exercises.explanation: 紅 + 色 = red color. 藍 + 色 = blue color.

exercises.prompt: In Chinese culture, red signals ___
Tap what you hear
Build "I like blue"
exercises.answer: 我 喜歡 藍 色

lessons.title: More colors

exercises.prompt: Which means "green"?
Which means "white"?
"黑" (hēi) means ___
the color
In Chinese culture, white is traditionally associated with ___
exercises.explanation: White is the funeral color in Chinese tradition. Don't gift white flowers or wear all white to a Chinese wedding.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 白 (bái) — white. Same syllable as 百 (bǎi, hundred), 拜 (bài, worship). Tones distinguish them.

exercises.prompt: "綠茶" (lǜ chá) means ___
exercises.explanation: 綠 = green, 茶 = tea. The unfermented variety, popular for daily drinking.

exercises.prompt: What does "紅茶" (hóng chá) literally translate to?
options: Red tea (= black tea in English)
exercises.answer: Red tea (= black tea in English)
exercises.explanation: Chinese names tea by the brewed color (red), English by the leaf color (black). Same drink, different perspective.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I like the white cat"
exercises.answer: 我 喜歡 白 色 的 貓
exercises.explanation: 白色的貓 — "of-white-color cat." 的 (de) attaches the color phrase to the noun.

exercises.prompt: "綠" (lǜ) means ___
Tap what you hear
Type the character meaning "black":
exercises.explanation: 黑 hēi — black.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Which means "grey"?
Build "I like green tea"
exercises.answer: 我 喜歡 綠 茶

exercises.prompt: "紅茶" literally translates to ___ tea
exercises.explanation: Chinese names this drink by brewed color; English by leaf color ("black").

exercises.prompt: Which color is associated with mourning in Chinese culture?
exercises.explanation: Avoid all-white at Chinese weddings.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Build "I like black tea" (literally "red tea")
exercises.answer: 我 喜歡 紅 茶
exercises.explanation: 紅茶 — what English calls "black tea."

exercises.prompt: What does "顏色" (yán sè) mean?
How do you ask "What color is it?"
Build "The apple is red"

exercises.explanation: 色 (sè) means "color" — pair with the color character.

exercises.prompt: How would you ask "What color is your car?"
exercises.explanation: Pattern: subject + 是 + 什麼顏色?

the colored object

exercises.prompt: To ask the color of something, use 什麼 + ___

exercises.prompt: "a red book" — most natural form?

exercises.prompt: What does "灰" (huī) mean?
Which means "purple"?
the color
"粉色" (fěn sè) means ___
exercises.explanation: 粉 = powder. "Powder color" — like rouge or makeup. The everyday word for pink.

exercises.prompt: Which means "orange color"?
exercises.explanation: 橙 (chéng) — also means the orange fruit. Same word in Mandarin for the fruit and the color.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Build: "I like the pink flower"
exercises.answer: 我 喜歡 粉 色 的 花

exercises.prompt: "棕色" (zōng sè) means ___
exercises.explanation: 棕 = palm tree (the brown trunk). Used for chocolate, soil, brown hair.

exercises.prompt: What does "灰色" (huī sè) mean?
exercises.explanation: 灰 (huī) literally "ash." Used metaphorically too: 灰心 ("ash heart") = discouraged.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 紫 (zǐ) — purple. Third tone, dipping.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My grandma's hair is grey"
exercises.answer: 我 奶奶 的 頭髮 是 灰 色
exercises.explanation: 頭髮 (tóu fa) = hair. 我奶奶的頭髮 = "my grandma's hair."

exercises.prompt: "A red car" — pick the correct one:
exercises.explanation: Most colors take 色 (color suffix) + 的 (modifier marker): 紅色的車. 紅的車 and 紅車 are sometimes acceptable in compounds but the full form is safest.

exercises.prompt: "The sky is blue" — which is correct?
exercises.explanation: Predicate adjectives in 是...的 take 的 at the end: 天是藍的. Dropping 的 (天是藍) sounds incomplete — like saying "the sky is blue thing" but trailing off.

exercises.prompt: Type the character meaning "purple":

the weather
What does "雲" (yún) mean?
"陰" (yīn) means ___
exercises.explanation: 陰 = shaded, overcast. The opposite of 晴 (sunny). Weather forecasts use 多雲 (mostly cloudy) and 陰 (overcast).

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 下 (xià) = come down/fall. 下雨 literally "rain falling." 下雪 = snowing.

exercises.prompt: Build: "Today the weather is good"
exercises.answer: 今天 天氣 很 好
exercises.explanation: Weather adjectives don't take 是. Use 很 + adjective.

exercises.prompt: What does "颳風" (guā fēng) mean?
exercises.explanation: 刮 = blow/scrape. 颳風 = the wind blows.

exercises.prompt: "天氣" (tiān qì) means ___
exercises.explanation: 天 = sky/day, 氣 = air. Together: "sky-air" = weather.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Type the character pair meaning "weather":
exercises.explanation: 天 (sky) + 氣 (air).

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear

exercises.explanation: 陰 yīn — shaded. 多雲 — partly cloudy.

exercises.prompt: Build "Today is sunny"
"颳風" (guā fēng) means ___
exercises.explanation: 刮 (blow) + 風 (wind).

the temperature word

exercises.explanation: Pleasantly warm — between cool and hot. The mid-range, comfortable temperature.

exercises.prompt: "涼快" (liáng kuai) means ___
exercises.explanation: Pleasantly cool — like a breeze on a hot day. Different from 冷 (cold/uncomfortable).

exercises.prompt: What does "春天" (chūn tiān) mean?

the season
Which means "summer"?

exercises.explanation: 秋 = harvest season. 天 = day/sky. Pattern across all seasons: season-character + 天.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear

exercises.prompt: "季節" (jì jié) means ___

exercises.prompt: In which season does it usually 下雪 (snow) in Beijing?

All four seasons end with the same character ___
exercises.explanation: 春天, 夏天, 秋天, 冬天 — each is season-character + 天 (day/sky). Easy pattern to remember.

guide.intro: A1 introduced 了 briefly. A2 is where it really earns its keep. There are also two siblings to learn — 過 (experience) and 還沒 (not yet) — that round out talking about the past.

sections.text: 了 — completed action
Tack 了 onto a verb to mark that the action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to a past tense, but technically it's an aspect marker — the action is complete, not necessarily long ago.

rows.translation: I am eating.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 飯。
rows.translation: I ate / I have eaten.
He came / he's here.

sections.text: Negation: 還沒 (not yet)
Don't pair 了 with 不/沒. To say "haven't done it", drop 了 and use 還沒 (hái méi):

rows.translation: I haven't eaten yet.
He hasn't come yet.

sections.text: 過 — experience marker
過 (guò) tags a verb as "have you ever done this in your life?" — it's about experience, not completion. Compare:

rows.source: 我 吃 過 北京 烤鴨。
rows.translation: I have eaten Peking duck (sometime).

rows.source: 我 吃 了 北京 烤鴨。
rows.translation: I ate Peking duck (just now).

sections.text: Rule of thumb: 了 = the action is wrapped up. 過 = at some point in your life this happened. They occasionally co-occur but you'll mostly pick one.

lessons.title: 著 — ongoing state
lessons.description: 著 marks a persisting state, not a progressive action.

exercises.prompt: Best English for "門 開 著"?

exercises.answer: The door is open (and stays open)
exercises.explanation: 著 (zhe) = the resulting state persists. Compare to 門 開 了 = the door opened.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a held / ongoing state?
options: 他 拿 著 一 本 書
他 拿 了 一 本 書
他 拿 過 一 本 書
他 要 拿 一 本 書
exercises.answer: 他 拿 著 一 本 書
exercises.explanation: 拿 著 = is holding (state). 拿 了 = picked up / took (event).

exercises.answer: A photo hangs / is hanging on the wall
exercises.explanation: 掛 著 + locative = stative description of how something is.

exercises.prompt: Which is the WRONG way to say "I'm reading a book right now"?
options: 我 在 看 書
我 正在 看 書
我 看 著 書

exercises.answer: 我 看 著 書
exercises.explanation: For action in progress use 在/正在. 著 is for stative descriptions.

lessons.title: Sentence-final 了
lessons.description: End-of-sentence 了 marks a change of state — different from verbal 了.

exercises.prompt: Best English for "我 累 了"?
options: I'm tired now / I've become tired
exercises.answer: I'm tired now / I've become tired
exercises.explanation: Sentence-final 了 after an adjective = change of state. New situation: I wasn't tired, now I am.

exercises.prompt: "下 雨 了" most naturally means:
options: It's started raining / It's raining now
exercises.answer: It's started raining / It's raining now
exercises.explanation: Sentence-final 了 marks the onset of a new state — the rain just began.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT a change-of-state 了?
options: 他 長大 了 (he's grown up)
我 餓 了 (I'm hungry now)
我 吃 了 飯 (I ate)
天 黑 了 (it's gotten dark)
exercises.answer: 我 吃 了 飯 (I ate)
exercises.explanation: 了 between verb and object marks COMPLETION, not change-of-state. The other three are change-of-state.

exercises.prompt: "我 不 想 吃 了" means ___
exercises.answer: I don't want to eat anymore
acceptableAnswers: I no longer want to eat
I don't feel like eating anymore
exercises.explanation: Sentence-final 了 with negation = shift away from a prior state.

exercises.answer: He has become a teacher (he wasn't before)
exercises.explanation: Sentence-final 了 + status noun = transition into that status.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence shows BOTH verbal 了 AND sentence-final 了?
options: 我 吃 了 飯 了 (I've eaten / done with the meal)
我 要 吃 飯 (I want to eat)
我 吃 過 飯 (I've eaten before)
exercises.answer: 我 吃 了 飯 了 (I've eaten / done with the meal)
exercises.explanation: First 了 = completion of eating; second 了 = current relevance / change-of-state "I'm done now".

lessons.title: 是…的 for emphasis

exercises.answer: It was yesterday that I went
exercises.explanation: 是…的 wraps the emphasized info (time, place, manner, etc.) about a known past event.

exercises.answer: 了 = neutral past report; 是…的 = emphasizes WHEN the event happened
exercises.explanation: Use 是…的 when the event itself is established and you want to highlight some detail like time, place, or how.

exercises.explanation: 的 closes the cleft at the end.

topics.title: Shopping
topics.description: Money, prices, and getting what you want

guide.intro: Real Chinese shopping is fast and friendly. Three phrases get you 80% of the way there: 多少錢 (how much), 太貴了 (too expensive), and 給我 (give me).

sections.text: Money words
Spoken Chinese uses 塊 (kuài) for the main currency unit; written and formal Chinese uses 元 (yuán). They're the same value — like "buck" vs "dollar". 毛 (máo) and 分 (fēn) are tenths and hundredths.
Asking the price

topics.title: Comparisons
topics.description: A is bigger than B — the 比 pattern

guide.intro: English uses "-er" or "more" for comparisons. Mandarin uses 比 (bǐ) — a single particle that does the same job, with a fixed word order: A 比 B + adjective.

sections.text: Basic pattern: A 比 B + adjective

rows.source: 我 比 他 高。
rows.translation: I am taller than him.

rows.source: 蘋果 比 香蕉 便宜。
rows.translation: Apples are cheaper than bananas.

rows.source: 今天 比 昨天 熱。
rows.translation: Today is hotter than yesterday.

sections.text: Don't add 很 / 不 / 是 to a 比 sentence. "我 比 他 很 高" is wrong — drop 很. The comparison itself does the work.
Even more: 更
Add 更 (gèng, "even more") before the adjective when comparing to an already-strong baseline:

rows.source: 他 比 我 更 高。
rows.translation: He is even taller than me.

sections.text: The most: 最
最 (zuì) before an adjective means "the most". No 比 needed — it's a superlative.

rows.translation: He is the tallest.

rows.source: 我 最 喜歡 茶。
rows.translation: I like tea the most.

sections.text: Negative: A 沒有 B + adjective
To say "A is NOT as ___ as B", flip to 沒有 (méi yǒu, "doesn't have"):

rows.source: 我 沒有 他 高。
rows.translation: I am not as tall as him.

topics.title: Connecting ideas
topics.description: And, but, because, so — stitch sentences together

guide.intro: Up to now most sentences have been one thought. A2 is where you start chaining: "I went and then I ate", "It rained but I went", "I'm tired because I worked". Mandarin makes this easy — a small set of connectors does most of the heavy lifting.

sections.text: 然後 — and then
然後 (rán hòu) chains two events in time. Use it to narrate sequences.

rows.source: 我 起床，然後 吃 早飯。
rows.translation: I get up, and then I eat breakfast.

sections.text: 但是 / 可是 — but
Both mean "but" with no real difference; 可是 is a touch more conversational.

rows.source: 我 想 去，但是 我 沒 時間。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dànshì wǒ méi shíjiān.
rows.translation: I want to go, but I don't have time.

sections.text: 因為...所以 — because...so
Mandarin often uses both halves where English uses just one ("I'm tired BECAUSE I worked" → 因為 我 工作 了，所以 我 很 累).

rows.source: 因為 下雨，所以 我 沒 去。
rows.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù.
rows.translation: Because it was raining, (so) I didn't go.

sections.text: You can drop one half if context is clear: "因為 下雨，我 沒 去" works too. The full pair just sounds slightly more emphatic.
或者 vs 還是 — both mean "or"
Easy mix-up. 或者 (huò zhě) goes in statements ("I want tea or coffee"). 還是 (hái shi) goes in questions ("Do you want tea or coffee?").

rows.source: 我 想 喝 茶 或者 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē chá huòzhě kāfēi.
rows.translation: I want to drink tea or coffee. (statement)

rows.source: 你 想 喝 茶 還是 咖啡？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng hē chá háishi kāfēi?
rows.translation: Do you want tea or coffee? (choice question)

topics.title: The 把 construction
topics.description: Putting the object first to talk about what you do TO it

guide.intro: 把 (bǎ) is one of the most distinctive features of Mandarin grammar. It moves the object before the verb to say "take X and do something to it". You'll hear it constantly — and English doesn't have a clean equivalent.

sections.text: The basic shape

Normal Chinese order is Subject–Verb–Object. With 把, you reorder to Subject–把–Object–Verb–(extra). The "extra" part is crucial — 把 sentences almost never end on a bare verb. There has to be a result, location, or change attached.

rows: 我 把 門 關 上
他 把 蘋果 吃 了
請 放 書 在 桌子 上
請 把 書 放 在 桌子 上

sections.text: When to use 把
Use 把 when you want to emphasize what HAPPENS TO a specific, known object — moving it, finishing it, changing it, putting it somewhere. Both speaker and listener know which object you mean.

rows.source: 我 把 作業 做 完 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuò wán le.
rows.translation: I finished the homework.

rows.source: 請 把 窗戶 打 開。
rows.translation: Please open the window.

rows.source: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Tā bǎ bēizi dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: He broke the cup.

sections.text: If you can't say what HAPPENS TO the object, don't use 把. "我 把 蘋果 喜歡" is wrong — 喜歡 (like) doesn't change the apple.
What can't follow 把
把 needs a verb that physically affects the object. Verbs that don't qualify: feeling/perception verbs (愛, 喜歡, 覺得, 知道), existence verbs (有, 是), and most stative or motion-only verbs (來, 去, 走).

rows.source: 我 喜歡 這 本 書。
rows.translation: I like this book. (NOT 我 把 這 本 書 喜歡)
He knows the answer. (NOT 他 把 答案 知道)

sections.text: Negation: 沒 / 不 goes BEFORE 把

rows.source: 我 沒 把 作業 做 完。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.
rows.translation: I didn't finish the homework.

rows.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào bǎ mén guān shàng.

topics.title: The 被 passive
topics.description: When something happens TO the subject — usually unpleasantly

guide.intro: 被 (bèi) is the passive marker — "got / was done by". It's the mirror image of 把: where 把 puts the actor first and the patient mid-sentence, 被 puts the patient (victim) first.

sections.text: The basic shape
Pattern: Patient + 被 + (Agent) + Verb + result. The agent is optional — drop it if it's unknown or obvious.

rows.source: 我 的 手機 被 偷 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.
rows.translation: My phone was stolen. (no agent)

rows.source: 杯子 被 他 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Bēizi bèi tā dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: The cup was broken by him.

rows.source: 錢 被 老闆 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Qián bèi lǎobǎn ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: The money was taken by the boss.

sections.text: 把 vs 被 — same event, different POV

rows: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了
杯子 被 他 打 破 了
小偷 偷 了 我 的 手機
我 的 手機 被 (小偷) 偷 了

sections.text: Mandarin's 被 has a slightly negative or unfortunate flavor — it's used much more often for bad things (got stolen, broken, scolded) than for neutral or good ones. Sentences like "I was praised" (我 被 表揚 了) work but feel marked.
叫 / 讓 — informal alternatives
In speech, 叫 (jiào) or 讓 (ràng) often replace 被. They sound more casual — but unlike 被, they REQUIRE an agent.

rows.source: 我 的 錢 讓 他 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de qián ràng tā ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: My money got taken by him.

rows.source: 他 叫 老師 批評 了。
rows.translation: He got scolded by the teacher.

sections.text: Negation
Same as 把 — put 沒 BEFORE 被.

rows.source: 我 的 手機 沒 被 偷。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi bèi tōu.
rows.translation: My phone wasn't stolen.

sections.text: Two flavors of 了
Mandarin uses 了 in two distinct slots, and 把 / 被 sentences often need both. Knowing which is which is the difference between a complete sentence and a fragment.

rows: Something is now different / new situation

rows.source: 他 吃 了 三 個 蘋果。
rows.pinyin: Tā chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
rows.translation: He ate three apples. (perfective 了₁ — action complete)
It's raining now. (sentence 了₂ — change of state, didn't use to be)

rows.source: 已經 下 了 三 天 雨 了。
rows.pinyin: Yǐjīng xià le sān tiān yǔ le.
rows.translation: It's been raining for three days. (BOTH 了 — completed duration AND ongoing relevance)

sections.text: Quick test: if the 了 hugs the verb (verb 了 object), it's 了₁. If the 了 is at the very end of the sentence, it's 了₂. Same character, different jobs.

topics.title: Giving with 給
topics.description: 給 as both "give" and a coverb meaning "for / to"

guide.intro: 給 (gěi) wears two hats. As a main verb it means "give". As a coverb sitting before another verb, it marks the recipient or beneficiary — "for someone", "to someone". Both uses are everywhere.

sections.text: 給 as main verb — "give"
Pattern: Subject + 給 + recipient + thing. Two objects in a row, recipient first.

rows.source: 我 給 他 一 本 書。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi tā yì běn shū.
rows.translation: I gave him a book.

rows.source: 媽媽 給 我 錢。
rows.translation: Mom gave me money.

sections.text: 給 as coverb — "for / to"
Sandwiched before another verb, 給 marks who benefits or receives the action. Pattern: Subject + 給 + recipient + verb + object.

rows.source: 我 給 你 買 了 一 杯 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ mǎi le yì bēi kāfēi.
rows.translation: I bought you a coffee. (the buying is FOR you)

rows.source: 他 給 媽媽 打 電話。
rows.translation: He's calling mom. (the call is TO mom)

rows.source: 請 給 我 介紹 一下。
rows.translation: Please introduce (it) to me.

sections.text: Notice how 給 you 買 (buy for you) and 給 媽媽 打 電話 (call mom) both keep 給 + person BEFORE the main verb. English flips this around — Chinese is rigid about the order.
Common 給-verb pairings

rows: 給 X 打 電話

topics.title: How well? — 得 complement
topics.description: Modify a verb with how it was done — 得 + adjective

guide.intro: 得 (de) lets you describe the manner or degree of an action: not WHAT you did, but HOW WELL or HOW MUCH. It's the closest Mandarin gets to English adverbs.

sections.text: The basic pattern
Pattern: Subject + Verb + 得 + (very) + Adjective. Note the position of 很 — almost always required to keep the sentence sounding natural.

rows.source: 他 跑 得 很 快。
rows.translation: He runs very fast.

rows.source: 她 唱 得 很 好。
rows.translation: She sings very well.

rows.source: 我 睡 得 不 好。
rows.translation: I didn't sleep well.

sections.text: When the verb has an object
If your verb takes an object, you have to repeat the verb. Mandarin can't have an object AND a 得 phrase on the same verb. Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object, Verb + 得 + adjective.

rows.source: 他 說 中文 說 得 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: He speaks Chinese very well. (literally: "speaks Chinese, speaks very well")

rows.source: 她 寫 字 寫 得 很 漂亮。
rows.pinyin: Tā xiě zì xiě de hěn piàoliang.
rows.translation: She writes characters beautifully.

sections.text: Common mistake: "他 說 中文 得 很 好" — wrong. The verb has to repeat. Or you can drop the object: "他 中文 說 得 很 好" also works.
Three different 得 / 的 / 地

rows: after a verb: how it was done
走 得 慢 — walks slowly

sections.text: All three are pronounced "de" (neutral tone) — only writing distinguishes them. Pay attention to position: 的 between nouns, 地 before verbs, 得 after verbs.
Negation: not 不 before 得 — 不 before the adjective

rows.source: 他 跑 得 不 快。
rows.translation: He doesn't run fast.

rows.source: 我 唱 得 不 好。
rows.translation: I don't sing well.

topics.title: Verb complements
topics.description: Resultative & directional complements — what English handles with separate words, Mandarin stitches onto the verb.

guide.intro: English says "I looked but didn't see it" with two verbs. Mandarin says 我 看 了 但 沒 看見 — the result (見 = perceive) is glued to the verb (看 = look). This is the resultative complement, and it's everywhere. Directional complements work the same way but for motion.

sections.text: Resultative complements
Verb + result. The verb is the action you tried; the second character tells the outcome. Without the complement, you're only saying you DID the action, not that it WORKED.
Directional complements
Verb + direction. 上 (up), 下 (down), 進 (in), 出 (out), 回 (back), 過 (across). Compound forms add 來 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker): 上來, 下去, 進來, 出去 …

rows.source: 他 走 上 樓。
rows.translation: He walks up the stairs.

rows.source: 他 走 上 來 了。
rows.translation: He walked up (toward me).

rows.source: 她 跑 出 教室。
rows.translation: She runs out of the classroom.

sections.text: Potential complement: 得 / 不

To say you CAN or CAN'T achieve the result, insert 得 (able) or 不 (not able) between the verb and the complement: 看得見 / 看不見, 聽得懂 / 聽不懂. This is NOT the same as 可以 + verb — that asks for permission. Potential complements ask whether the result is achievable.
English speakers reach for 可以 看見 ("can see"). That's wrong. Use 看得見 ("see-able") for "I can see it".

lessons.title: Resultative: 看見, 聽懂
lessons.description: Verb + result — actually saw, actually understood

exercises.prompt: Your friend says "我 看 了, 但 沒 看見". What happened?
options: She looked but didn't see it
exercises.answer: She looked but didn't see it
exercises.explanation: 看 = the action of looking. 看見 = look + perceive. 沒 看見 = didn't manage to see, even though she looked.

exercises.prompt: Which says "I heard (and understood) what the teacher said"?
options: 我 聽 老師 說 的 話
我 聽懂 老師 說 的 話 了

我 聽見 老師 但 不懂
exercises.answer: 我 聽懂 老師 說 的 話 了
exercises.explanation: 聽 = listen. 聽懂 = listen + understand. Without 懂, you've only listened — you might not have followed the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the result: "我 看 了 那 本 書, 但 沒 看 ___ 完" (I read that book but didn't finish)
exercises.explanation: 完 = finished. 看完 = read to completion. 沒 看完 = didn't finish reading.

exercises.prompt: Pick the contrast: "我 聽 了 這 首 歌" vs "我 聽懂 了 這 首 歌"
options: First = listened; second = listened AND understood
First is past, second is future
exercises.answer: First = listened; second = listened AND understood
exercises.explanation: 聽 alone is just the action. 聽懂 adds the result of comprehension.

exercises.prompt: Build "I didn't see her" (i.e. I looked but didn't manage to see her)

exercises.explanation: Negate the WHOLE resultative compound with 沒: 沒 看見, not 看 沒 見.

exercises.answer: 我 聽 不 懂 他
exercises.explanation: Potential complement: 不 sits INSIDE between verb and result. 聽不懂 = unable to understand by listening.

exercises.source: 我 看見 你 了
exercises.explanation: 看見 = the result was achieved — you were actually perceived. 了 marks the change of state.

exercises.prompt: "我 學會 了 開車" means:

I want to learn to drive
exercises.answer: I learned to drive (and can do it now)

exercises.prompt: "我 學完 了 這 本 書" means:
options: I finished studying this book (got to the end)
exercises.answer: I finished studying this book (got to the end)
exercises.explanation: 學完 = study + finish. Completion of the material, not necessarily mastery.

exercises.prompt: Contrast: "我 學完 了 中文" vs "我 學會 了 中文"

exercises.answer: First: I finished my Chinese course. Second: I actually know Chinese.
exercises.explanation: 完 = endpoint reached. 會 = ability acquired. You can finish a textbook without mastering the language.

exercises.prompt: "我 要 把 這 個 問題 學好" means:
options: I want to finish this topic
I want to study this topic well (thoroughly)

exercises.explanation: 學好 = study + well. 好 as a complement signals doing the action thoroughly / to a good standard.

exercises.source: 我 學會 彈 鋼琴 了

I learned how to play the piano
exercises.explanation: 學會 + verb-object = acquired the skill of doing X. 了 confirms the state change.

lessons.description: Verb + direction — walk up onto, take down, run out of

exercises.prompt: "她 跑 出 教室" means:
options: She runs out of the classroom

exercises.answer: She runs out of the classroom
exercises.explanation: 跑 = run; 出 = out. Verb + direction = motion + path.

exercises.prompt: Build "Please take the book down (off the shelf)"

exercises.prompt: Which means "He walks into the room"?

lessons.title: Compound directionals: 上來 / 下去 / 進來 / 出去
lessons.description: Add 來 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker)

exercises.prompt: You're upstairs. Your friend is downstairs. You shout "快 上來!" — what are you telling them?
exercises.explanation: 上來 = up + toward speaker. You're up; they're below; you want them to ascend to YOU.

exercises.prompt: You're upstairs and your friend wants to come up. They look up and say "我 上 ___ 了". Pick the right complement.
exercises.explanation: Speaker is moving TOWARD you (the listener, who is up). From their perspective, you are the destination — 來 (come). 上來 = coming up.

exercises.prompt: Contrast: "她 跑 出 去 了" vs "她 跑 出 來 了"
options: First: ran out (away from speaker). Second: ran out (toward speaker).
First: ran in. Second: ran out.
exercises.answer: First: ran out (away from speaker). Second: ran out (toward speaker).
exercises.explanation: 去 = away from speaker. 來 = toward speaker. The direction relative to YOU is the key insight English doesn't bake into motion verbs.

exercises.prompt: You're inside. Tell someone outside "Come in!"
exercises.explanation: 進來 = enter + toward speaker. Standard invitation to come inside.

exercises.prompt: You're inside. You tell a noisy person "出去!". What did you say?
exercises.explanation: 出去 = out + away from speaker. Sharp dismissal.

exercises.prompt: Build "He walked down (away from me)"
exercises.answer: 他 走 下 去 了
exercises.explanation: 下去 = down + away from speaker. 了 marks the completed motion.

exercises.explanation: 上來 (shàng lái) — come up. Common invitation when speaker is above the listener.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 出去 (chū qù) — please go out / leave. Contrast with 進來 (come in).

exercises.prompt: You're at the bottom of the stairs. You call to a friend at the top: "快 ___!" (Come down quickly!)
exercises.explanation: Speaker is below. Friend should DESCEND TOWARD speaker → 下來.

exercises.prompt: Your friend (inside) calls you (outside): "快 進 來 吧!" — what are they saying?
exercises.explanation: 進來 = enter + toward speaker. They're inside; you should enter TOWARD them.

exercises.answer: 來 = toward speaker; 去 = away from speaker

lessons.title: Potential: 看得見 vs 看不見
lessons.description: 得 / 不 inserted INSIDE the complement — not the same as 可以

exercises.prompt: "我 看得見 那 個 招牌" means:
options: I'm not allowed to see the sign

exercises.prompt: "我 聽不懂 他 說 的 話" means:
options: I refuse to listen to him

exercises.explanation: 聽不懂 = un-understandable-by-listening. 不 inserted between 聽 and 懂. The result isn't achievable.

exercises.prompt: English-L1 trap: which is WRONG for "I can see"?
options: Both 'B' and 'C' — use potential complement 看得見 for visibility
exercises.answer: Both 'B' and 'C' — use potential complement 看得見 for visibility
exercises.explanation: 可以 / 能 ask about PERMISSION or general capability. 看得見 specifically says "the sight reaches me / is visible." Native speakers say 看得見, not 可以 看見.

exercises.prompt: Fill in: "老師 的 字 太 小, 我 看 ___ 見" (I can't see — the writing is too small)
exercises.explanation: Negative potential: 看不見 = can't see. 不 goes between verb and complement.

exercises.prompt: Build "I can understand what you say"
exercises.answer: 我 聽得懂 你 說 的 話
exercises.explanation: 聽得懂 — single chunk: verb + 得 + result. Don't break it into 可以 + 聽懂.

exercises.prompt: "這 道 題 我 做 不 出 來" means:
options: I refuse to do this problem
I haven't done this problem yet
I can't figure out this problem (can't produce a solution)
exercises.answer: I can't figure out this problem (can't produce a solution)
exercises.explanation: 做不出來 = unable to produce / work out. 不 sits inside the verb-complement compound.

exercises.source: 我 看不見 黑板
acceptableAnswers: The blackboard isn't visible to me
exercises.explanation: 看不見 — classic complaint from the back of the classroom.

exercises.prompt: Pick the natural Mandarin for "I can hear it" (the sound reaches me):
exercises.explanation: 聽得見 = hear-able. Use for perception capability, not permission.

exercises.prompt: Form the question "Can you understand?" (comprehension):
options: 你 能 聽 嗎?
你 可以 聽 嗎?
你 想 聽 嗎?
exercises.explanation: 聽得懂 嗎 — standard "do you follow?" Distinct from asking permission.

exercises.prompt: Build "I can't finish this book" (don't have the ability to finish it)
exercises.answer: 我 看 不 完 這 本 書
exercises.explanation: 看不完 = can't finish reading. Different from 沒 看完 (haven't finished). 不 = capability; 沒 = past fact.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between 看見 and 看得見?
options: 看見 = past fact 'saw'; 看得見 = current capability 'can see'
exercises.answer: 看見 = past fact 'saw'; 看得見 = current capability 'can see'

我 可以 不 聽懂 新聞
聽 不 懂 新聞
exercises.answer: 我 可以 不 聽懂 新聞

exercises.prompt: Build "Please come in" (you're inside; addressee is outside)
exercises.explanation: 進來 = enter + toward speaker. Don't use 進去 here — that pushes them away from you.

exercises.prompt: Which is the natural way to say "I learned how to cook"?
options: 我 學 做 菜
我 學會 做 菜 了
我 可以 做 菜
我 想 學 做 菜
exercises.answer: 我 學會 做 菜 了
exercises.explanation: 學會 = study + acquired skill. The result (capability) is the point.

exercises.prompt: Trap: "我 沒 看見 你" vs "我 看 不 見 你" — pick the contrast.
options: First: didn't see you (past fact). Second: can't see you (capability now).
exercises.answer: First: didn't see you (past fact). Second: can't see you (capability now).
exercises.explanation: 沒 looks back at what happened. 不 inside the complement asks about current capability.

exercises.prompt: Build "She ran out of the house (toward us)"
exercises.answer: 她 跑 出 來 了
exercises.explanation: 跑出來 = run + out + toward speaker. 了 marks completion.

exercises.prompt: "作業 我 還 沒 做完, 但 已 經 做 ___ 一半" — fill in (already done half)
exercises.explanation: 已 經 做 了 一半 — neutral past with aspect 了. Don't add 完 if you haven't finished.

exercises.prompt: English-L1 trap: pick the WRONG translation of "I can hear the music"
options: 我 聽得見 音樂
我 能 聽到 音樂
我 可以 聽 音樂
Native uses 聽得見 / 聽到 — 可以 聽 means 'allowed to listen', a different idea
exercises.answer: 我 可以 聽 音樂
exercises.explanation: 可以 listen = have permission. Use a potential complement (聽得見) or 聽到 for actual perception.

topics.title: Measure word deep dive
topics.description: Beyond 個 — picking the right classifier for the noun: 條, 張, 只, 件, 把, 顆, 杯, 瓶 …

guide.intro: In A1 you learned 個 (the universal MW) and 本 (for books). Mandarin actually has hundreds of measure words — but you only need about a dozen to sound natural. The rule of thumb: shape and category of the noun pick the MW.

sections.text: Shape-based MWs

rows: fish, snakes, roads, pants, dogs (slim ones)

sections.text: Category MWs

rows: most animals; one of a pair

sections.text: Native speakers will understand if you say 一 個 魚 instead of 一 條 魚 — but you'll sound like a beginner. Picking the right MW is exactly what makes B1 sound like B1.
The 個 trap
English speakers over-use 個 because it's the safest fallback. Push yourself: when you see a long thin thing, reach for 條; flat → 張; clothing → 件; small round → 顆. Build the reflex.

lessons.title: 條 vs 張 — long vs flat
lessons.description: Shape decides — long-thin uses 條, flat-rectangular uses 張

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 魚 (one fish)
exercises.explanation: Fish are long and slender → 條. 一 條 魚.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 三 ___ 票 (three tickets)
exercises.explanation: Tickets are flat sheets → 張. 三 張 票.

exercises.prompt: Match the noun to its measure word
Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 路 (one road)
exercises.explanation: Roads are long and linear → 條. 一 條 路.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 兩 ___ 床 (two beds)
exercises.explanation: Beds are flat / broad surface → 張. 兩 張 床.

exercises.prompt: Match noun → MW
Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 圍巾 (one scarf)
exercises.explanation: Scarves are long thin strips → 條. 一 條 圍巾.

exercises.prompt: Trap: which MW DOESN'T fit "long, thin things"?
exercises.explanation: Paper is flat → 張 紙, not 條 紙. (Note: a long strip torn from paper could be 一 條, but for a sheet use 張.)

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW for "a long bench (long thin furniture)": 一 ___ 長椅
exercises.explanation: Long thin bench → 條. (A regular flat seat could use 張, but a long bench is shape-長.)

pairs.left: 裙子? (no — 件) — pants 褲子

exercises.explanation: Chinese has no plural -s, so English-L1 learners coming back from heavy MW practice sometimes forget plural marking. "three books" — count nouns with a number need -s.

lessons.title: 只 — animals & pairs
lessons.description: 只 for most animals and one-of-a-pair; 雙 for a pair

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 貓 (one cat)
exercises.explanation: Most animals → 只. 一 只 貓.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 兩 ___ 鞋 (two shoes — i.e. two singles)
exercises.explanation: Each shoe is one of a pair → 只. 一 雙 鞋 = one pair; 一 只 鞋 = one (single) shoe.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 鞋 (one PAIR of shoes)
exercises.explanation: 雙 = a pair. Compare 一 只 鞋 (one single shoe) vs 一 雙 鞋 (one pair).

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 鳥 (one bird)
exercises.explanation: Birds use 只 — most small/medium animals do.

exercises.prompt: "她 有 一 ___ 手 很 漂亮" — pick the right MW
exercises.explanation: Hands come as a pair → 雙 手 = (a pair of) hands.

exercises.prompt: Trap: pick the WRONG MW for animals
exercises.explanation: Don't use 個 for birds. 鳥 takes 只. (Dogs accept BOTH 只 and 條 — long thin dogs lean 條.)

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 筷子 (one pair of chopsticks)
exercises.explanation: Chopsticks come as a pair → 雙. One single chopstick (rare!) would be 一 只 筷子.

exercises.prompt: Fill in: "我 家 有 三 ___ 貓" (My family has three cats)
exercises.explanation: 三 只 貓 — animals take 只.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 兩 ___ 眼睛 (two eyes)
exercises.explanation: Each eye is one of a pair → 只 眼睛 (two singles). A pair → 一 雙 眼睛.

exercises.prompt: Which is the natural way to say "a pair of socks"?
exercises.explanation: Pairs (shoes, socks, gloves, chopsticks, hands, eyes) → 雙. Single sock → 只.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 老虎 (one tiger)
Build "There are five birds in the tree"

lessons.title: 件 — events & clothing
lessons.description: 件 for clothes (jacket, shirt) and abstract matters (一件事 = one thing/matter)

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 襯衫 (one shirt)
exercises.explanation: Most clothing items → 件. 一 件 襯衫.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 事 (one matter / one thing to discuss)
exercises.explanation: Abstract events / matters → 件. 一 件 事 = one matter. (一 個 事 sounds wrong.)

exercises.prompt: Fill in: "我 想 告訴 你 一 ___ 事" (I want to tell you one thing)
exercises.explanation: 件 事 = matter. Set phrase.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 三 ___ 外套 (three jackets)
exercises.explanation: Jackets, coats, shirts, dresses → 件.

exercises.prompt: Trap: which clothing item does NOT take 件?
exercises.explanation: Pants → 條 (long thin shape). Tops and jackets → 件. 一 條 褲子, 一 件 毛衣.

exercises.prompt: Fill in: "昨天 發生 了 一 ___ 大 事" (Yesterday a big thing happened)
exercises.explanation: Events / matters take 件. 一 件 大 事 = a big deal / important matter.

exercises.prompt: "He told me three ___" → 他 告訴 了 我 三 ___ 事
exercises.explanation: 三 件 事 = three matters / things to mention.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 這 ___ 工作 很 難 (this job is hard)
exercises.explanation: Jobs / tasks → 件 (treated as a matter). 一 件 工作.

English-L1 trap: which is WRONG?
exercises.explanation: Pens take 支 (zhī, for thin sticks) or 個 (casual). 件 is for clothing and matters, not stationery.

exercises.explanation: 杯 = cup of. 兩 杯 咖啡.

topics.title: Opinions & agreement
topics.description: I think, I believe, I agree — saying what you reckon

guide.intro: B1 means saying more than "I like" or "I want". You need ways to express opinions softly, agree, disagree, and ask people what THEY think. Three verbs do the heavy lifting: 覺得, 認為, and 看.

sections.text: 覺得 — feel / think (everyday)
覺得 (jué de) is the workhorse — "I feel / think that...". Use it for any soft, personal opinion. By far the most common in conversation.

rows.source: 我 覺得 這 個 電影 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zhè ge diànyǐng hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: I think this movie is good.

rows.source: 你 覺得 怎麼樣？
rows.translation: What do you think?

sections.text: 認為 — believe / hold (more formal)
認為 (rèn wéi) is firmer and more written — "I hold the view that...". Right for opinions on bigger issues, news, business, debate.

rows.source: 我 認為 這 個 計劃 不 行。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ rènwéi zhè ge jìhuà bù xíng.
rows.translation: I don't think this plan will work.

rows.source: 專家 認為 經濟 會 好轉。
rows.translation: Experts believe the economy will improve.

sections.text: 看 — see / view (informal opinion ask)
看 (kàn) literally means "look", but "你 看 …" idiomatically means "in your view, …". Used to gently ask someone's take.

rows.source: 你 看 我 該 怎麼 辦？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ kàn wǒ gāi zěnme bàn?
rows.translation: What do you think I should do?

rows.source: 我 看 應該 沒 問題。
rows.translation: I think it should be fine.

sections.text: Agreeing & disagreeing
Chinese conversation tends to soften disagreement. "我 不 太 同意" (I don't really agree) is gentler and more common than a flat "不 同意".
